items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: early seventies when Kissinger and Nixon came to visit to China. That began to loosen.

ctx.x: Were your parents interested in integrating themselves as much into American culture as they could? Or did they keep their own cultural identity intact?

Well they both spoke Cantonese, but because they were from different villages they didn’t speak together. But my mother, even though she still retains Cantonese at the third grade level, doesn’t speak to my daughter, who is in a Chinese immersion program. This was during a period, and still continues today in an English-only environment. And the assimilation process of Chinese-Americans was very distinct than say Japanese Americans in the way that Chinese-Americans or Chinese-Americans that lived in Chinatown,…

Yeah. I have this memory of having a write a report on Communist China in high school and having to get information from the London Embassy, because they didn’t have anything in the States here. Interesting how things change.

items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: day, I believe, that President Nixon made his visit to China.

ctx.x: Yeah. So how did I get to that. So anyway, I read a passage in Blues People by Leroi Jones, who is now known as Amiri Baraka. And in those days, I’m talking about the mid- 70’s, 1975, 1977, there were only two books on the reading list. There were probably a few more. But there was Blues People by Leroi Jones, and then The Music of Black Americans by Eileen Southern. So there weren’t that many. And I remember in the book by Amiri Baraka he talked about Africans brought over here as slaves, and they brought their…

day, I believe, that President Nixon made his visit to China. Before that, there wasn’t an open relationship between China and U.S. because of, you know, China being a communist government, the cold war period.

That’s a nice intersection of events. And it makes me think, I’m thinking about your composition process and the different musics that go into it. When I spoke — I did an interview with Toshiko Akiyoshi. And she had related when she was a kid, a child, she’s from Japan, but her father was working in China.
